draft.title: Roots of complex numbers
card: A non-zero complex number z has exactly n different nth roots. Write z = r cis θ. One root is r^(1/n) cis(θ/n).
The other roots come from adding 2π to the angle before dividing. The roots are r^(1/n) cis((θ + 2πk)/n) for k = 0, 1, ..., n − 1.
All n roots have the same modulus, r^(1/n). Their arguments are 2π/n apart, so they are evenly spaced on a circle centred at the origin.
Example: the cube roots of 1 have modulus 1 and arguments 0, 2π/3 and 4π/3. So they are 1, cis(2π/3) and cis(4π/3).
draft.remember: n roots, the same modulus, and arguments 2π/n apart.

a.q: The 5th roots of 1 are evenly spaced on a circle. What is the angle between neighbouring roots?
a.why: There are 5 roots spread evenly around a full turn of 2π, so neighbouring roots are 2π/5 apart. π/5 is tempting, but it would fit only 10 roots around the circle.
a.clue: Share one full turn equally between the roots.

b.q: The 4th roots of 16 are plotted in the complex plane. What are their modulus and the angle between neighbouring roots?
b.why: Each root has modulus 16^(1/4) = 2, because 2⁴ = 16. There are 4 roots, so neighbouring roots are 2π/4 = π/2 apart. Modulus 4 comes from dividing 16 by 4, which is not how roots work.
b.clue: Find the number that gives 16 when raised to the power 4.

problems.detail: "The other roots come from adding 2π to the angle before dividing" suggests adding 2π once. It should say adding multiples of 2π (2πk). The formula that follows corrects this, but the sentence on its own is imprecise.

final.title: Roots of complex numbers
card: A non-zero complex number \(z\) has exactly \(n\) different \(n\)th roots. Write \(z = r\,\text{cis}\,\theta\). One root is \(r^{\frac{1}{n}}\,\text{cis}\left(\frac{\theta}{n}\right)\).

The other roots come from adding multiples of \(2\pi\), written \(2\pi k\), to the angle before dividing by \(n\). The roots are \(r^{\frac{1}{n}}\,\text{cis}\left(\frac{\theta + 2\pi k}{n}\right)\) for \(k = 0, 1, \ldots, n - 1\).
All \(n\) roots have the same modulus, \(r^{\frac{1}{n}}\). Their arguments are \(\frac{2\pi}{n}\) apart, so they are evenly spaced on a circle centred at the origin.

Example: the cube roots of 1 have modulus 1 and arguments 0, \(\frac{2\pi}{3}\) and \(\frac{4\pi}{3}\). So they are 1, \(\text{cis}\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)\) and \(\text{cis}\left(\frac{4\pi}{3}\right)\).
final.remember: \(n\) roots, the same modulus, and arguments \(\frac{2\pi}{n}\) apart.

a.q: The 5th roots of 1 are evenly spaced on a circle. What is the angle between neighbouring roots?
a.why: There are 5 roots spread evenly around a full turn of \(2\pi\), so neighbouring roots are \(\frac{2\pi}{5}\) apart. \(\frac{\pi}{5}\) is tempting, but it would fit 10 roots around the circle.
a.clue: Share one full turn equally between the roots.

b.q: The 4th roots of 16 are plotted in the complex plane. What are their modulus and the angle between neighbouring roots?
b.why: Each root has modulus \(16^{\frac{1}{4}} = 2\), because \(2^{4} = 16\). There are 4 roots, so neighbouring roots are \(\frac{2\pi}{4} = \frac{\pi}{2}\) apart. Modulus 4 comes from dividing 16 by 4, which is not how roots work.
b.clue: Find the number that gives 16 when raised to the power 4.
